title: The world’s top-performing cities in 2026
gist: Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index shows New York, London and Paris entrenched at the top on economic scale and quality of life, while Shanghai, Delhi, Dubai, Riyadh, Warsaw and Prague are the fastest risers as growth shifts toward Asia, the Middle East and Central/Eastern Europe.

insights.claim: New York and London remain the top two cities in Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index, primarily because of the size of their economies and the strength of their labour markets.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Confirms these two hubs remain the base-case anchors for global capital, talent and corporate HQ location decisions in 2026.
insights.quote: New York and London remain at the pinnacle, largely due to the size of their economies and the strength of their labour market
insights.locator: New York and London remain at the pinnacle

insights.claim: Eight of the top 10 cities in the 2026 Global Cities Index are unchanged from the prior year's ranking, with Paris holding third place on strong quality-of-life scores.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Stability at the top signals low near-term rotation risk for investors anchoring real estate or corporate site-selection strategy to today's leading cities.
insights.quote: eight of the top 10 are unchanged from last year
insights.locator: Paris rounds off an unchanged top three

insights.claim: The world's leading cities show a resilience and self-reinforcing success that several years of weak growth or political upheaval have failed to fundamentally alter.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Suggests downside shocks (political instability, cyclical slowdowns) are unlikely to dislodge incumbent global hubs from long-term investment theses.
insights.quote: with several years of weak growth or political upheaval failing to fundamentally alter the nature of what makes these superstar cities attractive places to live and work
insights.locator: The enduring strength of these global leaders

insights.claim: The United States accounts for 30 of the top 100 cities in the index, with its strong showing driven specifically by the Economics and Human Capital categories rather than quality of life.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Signals the US city-growth story is an economic-scale and talent story, not a livability story — relevant for differentiating US urban investment theses from European ones.
insights.quote: the US alone accounting for 30 of the top 100 cities
insights.locator: cities across North America and Europe dominate

insights.claim: European cities' strong index performance is driven by outperformance in Quality of Life, Environment, and Governance categories, in contrast to the US's economics-and-talent-driven strength.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Investors comparing transatlantic urban markets should weight European cities' livability/governance edge against US cities' economic dynamism edge differently depending on the strategy (e.g., relocation-driven real estate demand vs. growth-driven office/labor demand).
insights.quote: In Europe, however, it is outperformance across the Quality of Life, Environmental, and Governance categories.
insights.locator: these differences are reflective of current trends

insights.claim: Strong performance by a city in one Global Cities Index category tends to elevate its performance in other categories, creating a virtuous cycle that allows the strongest cities to keep improving.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for screening which mid-ranked cities are likely to compound improvement versus stagnate — look for early cross-category gains as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: strong performance in one category tends to elevate performance in another, allowing the strongest cities to fall into virtuous cycles of improvement
insights.locator: the strength of these highflyers lies in their relatively broad success

insights.claim: Melbourne and Sydney dropped out of the Global Cities Index top 10 this year (falling to 13th and 16th) mainly due to weaker projected GDP and employment growth over the next five years, even as their broad-based scores remain strong.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Flags a near-term growth deceleration risk for Australia's two largest cities that could weigh on office and residential demand forecasts despite their still-solid overall index standing.
insights.quote: While Melbourne and Sydney drop out of the top 10 this year, largely due to weaker GDP and employment growth projections over the next five years, they continue to see strong broad-based performance and remain 13th and 16th, respectively.
insights.locator: Emblematic of this virtuous cycle are cities across Australia

insights.claim: All of Australia's cities featured in the Global Cities Index rank in the global top 100, with five of them in the top 50.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Indicates Australian urban markets broadly remain globally competitive even as the top two cities slip from the top 10.
insights.quote: all of Australia’s cities that feature in our index are in the top 100, with five in the top 50
insights.locator: In fact, all of Australia’s cities

insights.claim: Five of the ten largest projected GDP increases among global cities through 2050 are expected to occur in Asian cities.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Directs long-horizon capital toward Asian urban economies as the primary source of absolute GDP growth over the next quarter-century.
insights.quote: with five of the 10 largest GDP increases over the period to 2050 found here
insights.locator: The scale of growth occurring in Asia specifically

insights.claim: Shanghai, Beijing, and Delhi currently rank outside the top 100 of the Global Cities Index but are projected to see some of the largest GDP increases of any global city.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Highlights a valuation-gap opportunity: cities with low current index rank but outsized projected GDP growth could see disproportionate future demand for real estate, infrastructure, and services investment.
insights.quote: Shanghai, Beijing, and Delhi are all currently ranked outside the top 100 in our index, but they will see some of the largest increases in GDP.
insights.locator: The real story comes from Chinese and Indian cities

insights.claim: By 2050, the combined Chinese and Indian share of GDP across the major global cities tracked in the index is projected to exceed that of Europe.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A structural long-term thesis for reallocating urban/infrastructure exposure away from Europe and toward Chinese and Indian metros over a multi-decade horizon.
insights.quote: By 2050, we project the Chinese and Indian share of GDP across our major global cities to be above that of Europe
insights.locator: By 2050, we project the Chinese and Indian share

insights.claim: Shanghai's GDP is projected to overtake San Francisco's next year, despite Shanghai's economy having been only a quarter of its current size at the turn of the millennium.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A concrete, near-term (2027) milestone investors can watch to validate the broader China-urban-growth thesis.
insights.quote: Shanghai’s GDP is set to overtake San Francisco next year. This is despite Shanghai being just a quarter of its size at the turn of the millennium.
insights.locator: while Shanghai’s GDP is set to overtake San Francisco

insights.claim: Tokyo's substantial projected economic gains are more comparable to those of London and New York than to other Asian cities, reflecting its status as one of the largest and most advanced economies globally.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Cautions against grouping Tokyo with the high-growth emerging-Asia narrative; it should instead be benchmarked against mature Western superstar cities.
insights.quote: It is worth noting, however, that Tokyo’s substantial gains are more akin to London and New York’s than other Asian economies, given that the city is one of the largest and most advanced in the world.
insights.locator: It is worth noting, however, that Tokyo’s substantial gains

insights.claim: Dubai and Riyadh both entered the top 50 of the Global Cities Index this year, following decades of economic and social transformation in the region.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Marks a concrete inflection point where Gulf cities have crossed into the globally competitive tier, relevant for real estate and infrastructure allocators tracking Middle East urbanization.
insights.quote: Both Dubai and Riyadh have entered the top 50 this year
insights.locator: Cities across the Middle East are also increasingly prominent

insights.claim: Middle Eastern cities have used vast sovereign wealth funds to build infrastructure, improve quality of life, and attract top global talent and companies, driving their rise in the index.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Identifies sovereign wealth fund deployment as the key mechanism behind Gulf urban competitiveness, a factor to track for continued infrastructure and talent inflows.
insights.quote: Cities across the region have leveraged vast sovereign wealth funds to develop strong infrastructure, improve quality of life, and increasingly attract the world’s best and brightest workers and companies.
insights.locator: Cities across the region have leveraged vast sovereign wealth funds

insights.claim: The ongoing conflict in Iran poses a risk to the Middle East's successful urban growth model, even as Oxford Economics still expects the region's cities to drive significant growth overall.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A geopolitical risk flag for investors positioned in Gulf urban growth themes — the base case remains bullish but is not immune to regional conflict spillover.
insights.quote: While the conflict in Iran threatens to undermine this hugely successful growth model, we continue to expect cities across the Middle East to drive significant growth.
insights.locator: While the conflict in Iran threatens to undermine

insights.claim: Warsaw rose 109 places in the Global Cities Index over the past year, moving closer to the global top 50, on the back of strong economic and income growth.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: One of the sharpest single-year ranking moves cited in the report, useful as a headline data point for the Central/Eastern Europe convergence thesis.
insights.quote: Warsaw rose 109 places since last year, as it moved closer to the top 50
insights.locator: Strong economic and income growth has been central

insights.claim: Prague is currently the highest-ranked city in Central and Eastern Europe in the Global Cities Index, placing 51st overall this year.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Prague sits just outside the global top 50, making it a near-term candidate to watch for breaking into that tier.
insights.quote: Prague is the highest-ranked city in the region, placing 51st this year.
insights.locator: Prague is the highest-ranked city in the region

insights.claim: Oxford Economics projects that Prague, Warsaw, and Tallinn will top European economic growth rankings in the coming years, helping them close the gap on Western European peers.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Names specific Central/Eastern European cities as the projected fastest-growing in Europe — candidates for targeted regional real estate and business investment.
insights.quote: Our current projections suggest cities like Prague, Warsaw, and Tallinn will top European economic growth rankings in the coming years, helping them close the gap on their Western peers.
insights.locator: Our current projections suggest cities like Prague

insights.claim: Central and Eastern European cities' rise in the index caps off more than two decades of transformation since their accession to the European Union.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Frames EU accession as the long-run structural driver behind the region's urban convergence, useful context for assessing durability of the trend.
insights.quote: capping off over two decades of transformation since the ascension into the European Union
insights.locator: Strong economic and income growth has been central to these developments
